debate.situation: You are asking why places like Britain, Norway and Ireland have mild winters while Labrador or Hudson Bay, at similar latitudes, are brutally cold. The usual short answer credits the Gulf Stream, but the real explanation may be a mix of ocean currents, prevailing winds, mountains and the heat the sea stores. The decisive uncertainty is how much each factor contributes, since sources and models weigh them differently.

minds.title: The Ocean Advocate
minds.concern: Warm currents deliver real heat to Europe, and that delivery can change.
minds.author: Richard B. Alley

minds.title: The Old Navigator
minds.concern: The sea acts as a great conveyor of warmth, and its pathways can be charted from observation.
minds.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
minds.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea

minds.title: The Atmosphere Skeptic
minds.concern: Air, not water, carries most heat poleward, and winds decide who receives the ocean's warmth.
minds.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert

debate.speaker: The Old Navigator
debate.text: Start with the obvious: warm water leaves the tropics, runs up past Europe, and gives its heat to the air above. Canada has no such river of warmth on its east coast, only cold water coming down from the north. The sea explains the gap.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Too tidy. At these latitudes the air carries most of the poleward heat, not the water. A warm current is useless to Norway unless the wind pushes its warmth ashore. So the question becomes why the wind blows from sea to land in Europe.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Ocean Advocate
debate.text: Fair, but you are letting the ocean off too lightly. Even if the air does the carrying, the ocean is the furnace that fills it. And the evidence from past climate shows that when northern Atlantic circulation faltered, the region cooled sharply and fast.
debate.author: Richard B. Alley
debate.basis: Basis: Richard B. Alley, The Two-Mile Time Machine

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: Past collapses show the ocean can matter a great deal, not that it is the main cause today. Sea ice and shifting winds were tangled up in those episodes. I would go further than my source here: the wintertime story may be mostly about air, with the ocean as a supporting actor.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Old Navigator
debate.text: Then explain the wind itself. Westerlies cross the Atlantic and arrive in Europe already softened by the water they passed over. In Canada the same westerlies arrive from the continent, so a cold interior sends cold air out to the east coast. Same wind, different history.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: That is a point for me, and it narrows your claim. The ocean matters by storing summer heat and releasing it slowly into winter air, not only by streaming north. And large mountain ranges such as the Rockies bend the wind pattern so that cold air tends to spill down over eastern North America.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Ocean Advocate
debate.text: Notice what just happened. You gave away the pure wind story, and I will give away the pure Gulf Stream story. Heat storage, a warm current, mountains and wind direction all work together. The honest version is a bundle, and the Gulf Stream is one strand, not the whole rope.
debate.author: Richard B. Alley
debate.basis: Basis: Richard B. Alley, The Two-Mile Time Machine

debate.speaker: The Old Navigator
debate.text: A bundle is fine, but do not lose the practical lesson. Sailors and farmers do not care about the ranking of causes. They care that the water off Europe is warm and the water off Labrador is cold, and that you can measure this.
debate.author: Matthew Fontaine Maury
debate.book: The Physical Geography of the Sea
debate.basis: Basis: Matthew Fontaine Maury, The Physical Geography of the Sea

debate.speaker: The Atmosphere Skeptic
debate.text: And I will push back on that. Measuring a warm current is not the same as proving it causes the mild winters. If a quarter of the effect is ocean and the rest is wind and storage, a headline crediting the current alone teaches the wrong lesson.
debate.author: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert
debate.basis: Basis: Raymond T. Pierrehumbert, Principles of Planetary Climate

debate.speaker: The Ocean Advocate
debate.text: I will not defend the headline, but I will defend the stakes. If the ocean share is small, a slowdown of the Atlantic circulation is a modest worry. If it is larger than your estimate, it is a serious one. That disagreement is still open, and it is the part worth watching.
debate.author: Richard B. Alley
debate.basis: Basis: Richard B. Alley, The Two-Mile Time Machine

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the gap is not one cause but a pattern: air that reaches Europe has crossed a warm, heat-storing ocean, while air reaching eastern Canada has crossed a cold continent shaped by mountains and winds. What remains disputed is how large the share of the Gulf Stream and wider Atlantic circulation is compared with the atmosphere, and therefore how much a change in the ocean would matter. A possible self-reflection is whether the single-cause version you first heard felt satisfying because it was simple.
debate.dependsOn: If you want a simple, defensible answer, say that prevailing winds carry ocean-moderated air onto Europe and continental air onto eastern Canada, with warm Atlantic water helping. If you care about what could change in the future, the size of the ocean's own contribution becomes the key fact, because a large share makes shifts in Atlantic circulation more consequential. If that share is unknown to you, a proportionate way to learn it is to look for climate model studies that compare the same region with and without ocean heat transport, and check whether they agree.
